params.question: A patient with anaemia has a reticulocyte production index (RPI) of 0.8. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemolysis triggers a vigorous marrow response, producing an RPI of 2 or above. A low RPI rules out a hyperproliferative cause.

answers.text: Acute blood loss stimulating increased marrow output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acute blood loss also drives the marrow to increase output, producing an RPI of 2 or above — not 0.8.

answers.text: Bone marrow hypoproliferation from a deficiency state or marrow suppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An RPI below 2 means the marrow is not compensating adequately, pointing to iron, B12 or folate deficiency, renal failure, or primary marrow suppression.
Splenic pooling alone does not produce a low RPI. Conditions with splenomegaly and haemolysis typically show an elevated RPI.

overallFeedback.feedback: An RPI below 2 indicates hypoproliferation — the marrow is not compensating adequately. Haemolysis and acute blood loss both produce an RPI of 2 or above because the marrow responds vigorously.
Correct. An RPI below 2 signals hypoproliferation — the marrow is underperforming. Combined with MCV, this two-axis framework narrows the differential to specific causes.

interactions.label: In anaemia of chronic disease, serum ferritin is typically low because iron stor

params.question: In anaemia of chronic disease, serum ferritin is typically low because iron stores are depleted.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: In anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is actually normal or elevated. Interleukin-6 drives hepcidin production, which traps iron inside macrophages — the iron is sequestered, not depleted. Low ferritin points to iron deficiency anaemia, making this the crucial distinguishing test.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. In anaemia of chronic disease, hepcidin traps iron inside macrophages, so ferritin is normal or elevated. Iron is sequestered, not depleted. This is the key differentiator from iron deficiency anaemia, where ferritin is genuinely low.

interactions.label: A 52-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor without jaundice, and melaena. H

params.question: A 52-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor without jaundice, and melaena. His haemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL, MCV is 68 fL, and serum ferritin is low. After confirming iron deficiency anaemia, what should the clinician prioritise next?

answers.text: Start oral iron replacement and review in three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting iron alone without investigating the cause of bleeding in a middle-aged man with melaena risks missing a gastrointestinal malignancy — the dangerous diagnosis hiding behind the obvious label.

answers.text: Order haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia trait

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ferritin is already low, confirming iron deficiency. Thalassaemia trait presents with normal ferritin, so electrophoresis is not the priority here.
Correct. Safety-netting requires excluding dangerous diagnoses even when a benign cause is apparent. In a middle-aged man with melaena, gastrointestinal malignancy must be excluded.

answers.text: Check serum vitamin B12 and folate levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The MCV of 68 fL indicates microcytic anaemia. B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytic anaemia (MCV above 100 fL), so these tests are not relevant here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed, but the clinical story does not end there. In a 52-year-old man with melaena, safety-netting demands investigation for gastrointestinal malignancy — the dangerous diagnosis hiding beneath the obvious one.

Correct. This is safety-netting in action — iron deficiency anaemia is the haematological classification, but gastrointestinal malignancy is the diagnosis that cannot be missed in a middle-aged man with melaena.

interactions.label: In which of the following clinical scenarios is bone marrow aspiration most appr

params.question: In which of the following clinical scenarios is bone marrow aspiration most appropriately indicated?

answers.text: A young woman with microcytic anaemia and a markedly low serum ferritin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Low ferritin already confirms iron deficiency as the cause. The diagnosis is established, and bone marrow aspiration would not add useful information.

answers.text: A patient with macrocytic anaemia and elevated serum methylmalonic acid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elevated methylmalonic acid is the most specific confirmatory test for vitamin B12 deficiency. The diagnosis is clear without bone marrow examination.

answers.text: Unexplained pancytopaenia that has not responded to empirical treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bone marrow aspiration is reserved for situations where simpler tests have not yielded a diagnosis — unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected marrow infiltration, or treatment-refractory anaemia.

answers.text: Normocytic anaemia in a patient with known chronic kidney disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mechanism is clear — reduced erythropoietin production by the diseased kidneys. Bone marrow aspiration is unnecessary when the aetiology is already explained.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bone marrow aspiration is reserved for situations where simpler investigations have not established the diagnosis — unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected marrow infiltration, or anaemia that fails to respond to appropriate treatment.

Correct. Bone marrow aspiration is not a shortcut around interpreting simpler tests. It is indicated when the diagnosis remains unexplained after standard investigations — such as in unexplained pancytopaenia or treatment-refractory anaemia.

interactions.label: A community health worker is planning iron and folic acid supplementation under

params.question: A community health worker is planning iron and folic acid supplementation under the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme. Which schedule is correct for a 24-year-old pregnant woman?

answers.text: Weekly iron and folic acid tablets throughout pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Weekly supplementation is the Anaemia Mukt Bharat schedule for adolescents, not for pregnant women. Pregnant women need daily tablets because of increased iron demands during gestation.

answers.text: Daily iron and folic acid tablets throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Under the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme, pregnant women receive daily iron and folic acid throughout pregnancy and continuing for 180 days postpartum to rebuild depleted stores.

answers.text: Iron tablets only during the first trimester

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron demands increase progressively through gestation and into lactation. Supplementation must continue throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum, not just the first trimester.

answers.text: Monthly intramuscular iron injections from the second trimester onward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The programme uses oral iron and folic acid tablets for routine supplementation, not intramuscular injections. Parenteral iron is reserved for cases of oral intolerance or malabsorption.

overallFeedback.feedback: Under the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme, pregnant women receive daily iron and folic acid throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum. The weekly schedule is reserved for adolescents.

Correct. The Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme prescribes daily iron and folic acid for pregnant women throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum — in contrast to the weekly schedule for adolescents.
